rules.title: Just cause required for covered tenancy terminations
rules.requirement: Landlords may terminate a tenancy covered by the JCO only for a qualifying just cause.
rules.key_value: Six months of occupancy or expiration of the original lease, whichever comes first
rules.coverage_conditions: Residential rental properties in the City of Los Angeles that are not regulated by the City's RSO, once the tenant has occupied the same unit for at least six months or the original lease has expired, whichever occurs first. The source identifies exceptions, expressly not exhaustive, for transient hotels, licensed care facilities, fraternity or sorority houses, an owner's roommate, cooperatives under certain circumstances, some nonprofit homeless facilities or short-term substance-abuse treatment centers, and some HACLA or government-owned properties. The qualifications for these exceptions require review. Buildings newer than October 1, 1978 and properties containing only one single-family dwelling can be covered.
rules.exemptions: The identified property and tenancy exceptions are preserved in coverage_conditions. Listed at-fault grounds are nonpayment of rent, failure to cure a rental-agreement violation, nuisance or property damage, illegal use, failure to renew a similar agreement, failure to provide reasonable access, and an unapproved subtenant remaining at lease end. Listed no-fault grounds are occupancy by the owner or an immediate family member; occupancy by a resident manager when required by law, an affordable housing covenant or regulatory agreement; demolition, permanent removal from the rental market or conversion to nonresidential use; a government order to vacate; HUD ownership and sale; residential hotel conversion or demolition; and conversion to affordable housing. The source does not establish the detailed prerequisites for each ground.
rules.citation: Los Angeles Just Cause for Eviction Ordinance; LAHD guidance, Rental Units Covered Under JCO and Legal Reasons for Eviction
rules.quoted_span:
If you own rental property in the City of Los Angeles, it may be subject to the
Just Cause Ordinance
(JCO).  It prohibits terminations of tenancies without just cause and requires relocation assistance for no-fault evictions.
Rental Units Covered Under JCO
The JCO covers most residential properties in the City of Los Angeles that are not regulated by the City’s Rent Stabilization Ordinance (RSO).
In order to apply to a tenancy, it requires that the tenant either has lived in the same unit for at least six months or that their original lease expired, whichever comes first.  There are other specific exceptions to the JCO including, but not limited to, transient hotels, licensed care facilities, fraternity or sorority houses, owner’s roommate, cooperatives under certain circumstances, some non-profit facilities for the homeless or short-term treatment centers for substance abuse, and some properties owned by HACLA or the government.  The JCO can apply to buildings that are newer than October 1, 1978.  The JCO can apply to a property that contains only one single-family dwelling.
Legal Reasons for Eviction
Tenant i
s at-fault
Under the JCO, the landlord may recover possession of a rental unit
in specific situations. Below is a list of reasons for which a tenant could be evicted and
would be considered at fault
. If the tenant is at fault
for the eviction, then the tenant will not be entitled to relocation assistance.
Failure to pay rent
Failure to cure a violation of the rental agreement
Creating a nuisance or causing damage to the property
Using the rental unit for an illegal purpose
Failure to renew a similar rental agreement
Failure to provide the landlord with reasonable access to the rental unit
The person at the end of the lease term is a subtenant not approved by the landlord
Tenant is not at-fault
Situations in which the property owner wishes to regain the use of the rental unit, as the result of a personal or business decision, and
not the
tenant’s fault, may be cause for eviction, but the property owner may have to pay the tenant
relocation assistance
. These reasons include
The
owner or an immediate family member
will move into the rental unit
Resident manager will move into the rental unit when required by law or by an affordable housing covenant or regulatory agreement
Demolition, permanent removal from the rental market, or conversion to
non-residential
Government order to vacate
HUD owns and is selling the property
Residential Hotel being converted or demolished
Conversion to affordable housing

rules.title: Relocation assistance for qualifying no-fault evictions
rules.requirement: Property owners must provide relocation assistance for no-fault evictions that qualify for assistance under the JCO. Tenants evicted for an at-fault reason are not entitled to that assistance.
rules.coverage_conditions: Residential rental properties in Los Angeles outside the City's RSO, after the tenant has lived in the same unit for at least six months or the original lease has expired, whichever occurs first. Exceptions include transient hotels, licensed care facilities, fraternity or sorority houses, an owner's roommate, certain cooperatives, some nonprofit homeless facilities or short-term substance-abuse treatment centers, and some HACLA or government-owned properties; the source makes this list nonexhaustive and leaves several qualifications unspecified. Newer buildings and properties containing only one single-family dwelling can be covered. Any additional tenancy or property eligibility conditions for relocation assistance require review because the source says owners may have to pay without supplying those details.
rules.exemptions: At-fault evictions do not entitle the tenant to relocation assistance. Potential no-fault grounds listed are owner or immediate-family occupancy; resident-manager occupancy required by law, an affordable housing covenant or regulatory agreement; demolition, permanent removal from the rental market or conversion to nonresidential use; a government order to vacate; HUD ownership and sale; residential hotel conversion or demolition; and conversion to affordable housing. The source does not specify payment amounts or establish that every listed no-fault eviction requires payment.

rules.title: Post and provide the Notice of Right to Counsel
rules.requirement: Landlords must post a Notice of Right to Counsel in a conspicuous common area of the residential building where the tenant resides. They must also provide it to the tenant at the beginning of the tenancy and whenever an eviction notice is served.
rules.citation: LAHD JCO guidance, Required Registration and Posted Notification
rules.quoted_span:
Beginning August 20, 2025, landlords must post a
Notice of Right to Counsel
in a conspicuous common area of the residential building where the tenant resides. This notice is also to be provided to the tenant at the beginning of the tenancy and anytime an eviction notice is served.

rules.title: Provide and post the Notice of Renters’ Protections
rules.requirement: All landlords of residential properties must provide a Notice of Renters’ Protections to tenants who begin or renew their tenancy on or after January 27, 2023. Landlords must also post the notice in an accessible common area of the property.
rules.coverage_conditions: All residential rental properties in Los Angeles are within the stated posting scope; individual delivery is required for tenants whose tenancy begins or renews on or after January 27, 2023. The allowed facts cannot represent that tenancy commencement or renewal date.
rules.exemptions: The source states no exemption from this notice duty; the January 27, 2023 tenancy commencement or renewal condition applies to individual delivery.
rules.citation: LAHD JCO guidance, Required Registration and Posted Notification
rules.quoted_span: All landlords of residential properties must provide a Notice of Renters’ Protections to tenants who begin or renew their tenancy on or after January 27, 2023. This notice must also be posted in an accessible common area of the property.

rules.title: Rent arrears must exceed Fair Market Rent for nonpayment eviction
rules.requirement: Landlords of RSO or JCO rental units may not evict a tenant for falling behind in rent unless the amount owed exceeds the Fair Market Rent applicable to the unit’s bedroom size.
rules.key_value: Rent owed must exceed bedroom-size Fair Market Rent
rules.coverage_conditions: Rental units in Los Angeles covered by either the City's RSO or JCO. The source does not define RSO eligibility. For the JCO branch, the source describes residential properties outside the RSO and a tenant who has lived in the same unit for at least six months or whose original lease has expired, whichever occurs first; it also identifies nonexhaustive exceptions for transient hotels, licensed care facilities, fraternity or sorority houses, an owner's roommate, certain cooperatives, some nonprofit homeless facilities or short-term substance-abuse treatment centers, and some HACLA or government-owned properties. Those exception qualifications and the RSO branch require review.
rules.exemptions: This is a restriction on nonpayment evictions, not a statement that exceeding the threshold independently authorizes eviction. The source provides no current bedroom-specific FMR amounts.
rules.citation: LAHD JCO guidance, Evictions for Non-Payment of Rent
rules.quoted_span: Applies to all RSO & JCO rental units. Effective March 27, 2023, landlords may not evict a tenant who falls behind in rent unless the tenant owes an amount higher than the Fair Market Rent (FMR). The FMR depends on the bedroom size of the rental unit.

rules.title: File eviction notices with LAHD
rules.requirement: Landlords issuing eviction notices for JCO or RSO rental properties must file those notices with LAHD within three business days after service on the tenant.
rules.coverage_conditions: Los Angeles rental properties covered by the JCO or RSO. RSO coverage criteria are not supplied. The JCO scope described in this source is residential rental property outside the RSO, with tenant occupancy of at least six months or expiration of the original lease, whichever occurs first, and nonexhaustive exceptions for transient hotels, licensed care facilities, fraternity or sorority houses, an owner's roommate, certain cooperatives, some nonprofit homeless facilities or short-term substance-abuse treatment centers, and some HACLA or government-owned properties. Review is needed to establish the unspecified exception qualifications and whether the JCO tenancy waiting period also limits this property-level filing duty.
rules.exemptions: The passage expressly identifies JCO and RSO rental properties as its scope, despite subsequently referring to all eviction notices issued in the City.
rules.citation: LAHD JCO guidance, Eviction Notices Filed with LAHD
rules.quoted_span: Applies to all JCO & RSO rental properties – All eviction notices issued to tenants in the City of Los Angeles must be filed with LAHD within three (3) business days of service on the tenant.

review.issue: The JCO coverage exceptions are expressly nonexhaustive, and several are only partially described. Complete executable coverage cannot be established from this capture; do not infer that an address lacks an exemption.
review.quoted_span: In order to apply to a tenancy, it requires that the tenant either has lived in the same unit for at least six months or that their original lease expired, whichever comes first.  There are other specific exceptions to the JCO including, but not limited to, transient hotels, licensed care facilities, fraternity or sorority houses, owner’s roommate, cooperatives under certain circumstances, some non-profit facilities for the homeless or short-term treatment centers for substance abuse, and some properties owned by HACLA or the government.

review.issue: The source describes the JCO just-cause and relocation duties as current but supplies no precise effective date for them. Their effective_date values remain null; the page publication and modification dates are not enactment or effective dates.

review.issue: The relocation discussion does not provide amounts, deadlines, or the full conditions distinguishing no-fault evictions that require assistance from those that do not. No payment amount or universal entitlement for every listed no-fault ground is established.

Their effective dates and detailed registration scope are not established here.

All properties rented or offered for rent must be

review.issue: The filing duty has no precise effective date in the capture. Its opening property-level scope and the JCO's tenancy-level waiting period require review before treating that waiting period as a filing exemption.

review.issue: The supplied AB 1482 discussion concerns independently governed California law and must be extracted from an appropriate state source. Do not relabel it as a Los Angeles ordinance; the quoted percentage periods also precede the as-of date and do not establish a current percentage.
review.quoted_span:
When Can Rent Be Increased Under State Law AB1482
The JCO does not regulate rent increases, however, state law
AB 1482, the California Tenant Protection Act of 2019
,
may regulate the rent amount in buildings that are older than 15 years old.
Effective August 1, 2024 to July 31, 2025, the maximum allowable increase is
8.9%
.
Previously, from August 1, 2023 to July 31, 2024 the maximum annual increase for units subject to AB 1482 was 8.8%
.
(
A
nnual rent increases are limited to no more than 5% plus the percentage change in the cost of living for the region in which the property is located, or 10% whichever is lower).

review.issue: The AB 1482 property, affordability, dormitory, owner-occupancy, ownership, notice, separate-sale and RSO exceptions belong to the state-law discussion. They must not be imported as JCO exemptions; the source expressly distinguishes single-family homes and condominiums from JCO exemption.
review.quoted_span:
Properties
not
covered under AB 1482:
-Units that were constructed within the last 15 years (this applies on a rolling basis – i.e.. a unit constructed on January 1, 2006 is not covered as of January, 1 2020, but is covered on and after January 1, 2021).
-Units restricted by a deed, regulatory restrictions, or other recorded document limiting the affordability to low or moderate-income households.
-Certain dormitories.
-A two-unit property, provided the second unit was occupied by an owner of the property for the entire period of the tenancy.
-Single-family homes and condominiums are only exempt from state law but not the JCO if both
(A)
and
(B)
apply:
(A)
the property is
not
owned by one of the following:
(i) a real estate trust, or
(ii) a corporation, or
(iii) an LLC with at least one corporate member.
—–AND—-
(B)
The landlord notified the tenant
in writing
that the tenancy is not subject to the “just cause” and rent increase limitations as specifically described in Civil Code Sections 1946.2(e)(8)(B)(i) and 1947.12(d)(5)(B)(i).
-The limited exemption for single-family homes does not apply where there is more than one dwelling unit on the same lot, or any second residential unit in the building that cannot be sold separately from the subject unit (such as an in-law unit).
-Units that are already subject to the City’s RSO.

review.issue: The source supplies no operative duties or affirmative no-rule findings for security_deposits, application_screening_fees, screening_restrictions, or algorithmic_rent_setting. Its silence does not establish the absence of applicable law in those categories.
